title: Ski Jumping: training overview
d: Ski Jumping training builds the fitness, skills, and tactics the rules demand.
definition: Ski Jumping training builds the fitness, skills, and tactics the rules demand.
description: Ski Jumping training has three pillars: the physical engine, the technical skills, and the tactical brain. The rules define the demands — individual over jumps last ~5 seconds of flight — and training reverses them into a program: energy systems for the duration, strength for the collisions and jumps, skills for the techniques, tactics for the decisions. This database covers all four across a season, from first preseason week to championship taper.

Test the systems with time trials and heart-rate data, then target the weakest one first; the fittest athlete is rarely the winner, but the unfittest never is.

title: Strength program
d: Ski Jumping strength work: Sprint power and neck strength: 30m fly times predict start performance..
definition: Ski Jumping strength work: Sprint power and neck strength: 30m fly times predict start performance..
description: Strength training for Ski Jumping: Sprint power and neck strength: 30m fly times predict start performance. Train strength twice a week in season, three times out of it. Lift for the sport, not for the mirror — every exercise should answer which on-field action it improves. Keep a training log; progressive overload over months is what separates good from great.

title: Conditioning plan
d: Ski Jumping conditioning mirrors jumps last ~5 seconds of flight: work-to-rest matched to the game clock.
definition: Ski Jumping conditioning mirrors jumps last ~5 seconds of flight: work-to-rest matched to the game clock.
description: Conditioning for Ski Jumping must mirror the game clock: jumps last ~5 seconds of flight. Build the aerobic base first — it speeds recovery between hard efforts — then layer sport-specific intervals. Never sacrifice skill sessions for extra running; tired athletes learn bad technique. Monitor with resting heart rate and repeat-sprint tests.

title: Skill acquisition
d: Learn Ski Jumping skills in three stages: grooved, pressured, then match-random.
definition: Learn Ski Jumping skills in three stages: grooved, pressured, then match-random.
description: Skill learning in Ski Jumping follows blocked-to-random progression: first groove the movement alone, then add pressure, then randomize like a match. Ten thousand mindless reps engrave errors; one thousand deliberate reps with feedback engrave skill. Film everything — athletes cannot fix what they cannot see.

title: Tactical training
d: Ski Jumping tactics are rehearsed, not improvised: walk, jog, full speed, then live.
definition: Ski Jumping tactics are rehearsed, not improvised: walk, jog, full speed, then live.
description: Tactical training in Ski Jumping: walk through the shape, jog it, run it full speed, then go live. Tactics fail when players think instead of recognize — so rehearse until recognition is instant. Review film weekly: pause at decisions and ask what the right choice was before revealing it.

title: Sports nutrition
d: Fuel Ski Jumping: carbs for the work, protein for repair, timing around sessions.
definition: Fuel Ski Jumping: carbs for the work, protein for repair, timing around sessions.
description: Nutrition for Ski Jumping athletes: carbohydrate covers the training load, protein (about 1.6-2.2 g per kg daily) repairs it, and fluids with electrolytes cover the sweat. Eat a familiar meal 3 hours before competition and a carb-protein mix within 2 hours after. Supplements are the last one percent — food is the other ninety-nine.

title: Hydration plan
d: Ski Jumping hydration: start hydrated, drink to thirst plus plan, replace after.
definition: Ski Jumping hydration: start hydrated, drink to thirst plus plan, replace after.
description: Hydration for Ski Jumping: weigh before and after sessions to learn your sweat rate, drink on a schedule in long events, and replace sodium in heat. Losing two percent of body mass to dehydration measurably impairs skill and decisions. Practice the race-day drinking plan in training — never try anything new on competition day.

title: Recovery methods
d: Recover from Ski Jumping: sleep first, then easy movement, food, and stress control.
definition: Recover from Ski Jumping: sleep first, then easy movement, food, and stress control.
description: Recovery from Ski Jumping training ranks: sleep (8-9 hours for athletes) first, then light movement, then nutrition timing, then stress management. Ice baths and gadgets are minor compared to sleep. Track morning readiness — soreness, mood, resting heart rate — and adjust the day's load to it.

title: Sleep for athletes
d: Ski Jumping athletes need 8-9 hours: sleep is when training adaptations happen.
definition: Ski Jumping athletes need 8-9 hours: sleep is when training adaptations happen.
description: Sleep is the legal performance enhancer for Ski Jumping: growth hormone peaks in deep sleep, skills consolidate overnight, and reaction time degrades measurably with debt. Keep the room cool, dark, and screen-free; keep wake time consistent even on weekends. Naps of 20-30 minutes help; long late naps hurt night sleep.

title: Mental skills
d: Train the Ski Jumping mind: routines, self-talk, visualization, and pressure rehearsal.
definition: Train the Ski Jumping mind: routines, self-talk, visualization, and pressure rehearsal.
description: Mental training for Ski Jumping: a pre-performance routine that never changes, self-talk that is instructional not emotional, visualization of successful execution, and deliberate pressure practice. Confidence comes from preparation evidence — keep a log of good sessions to read before big events. Anxiety is normal; unmanaged anxiety is optional.

title: Season planning
d: Plan the Ski Jumping year: base, build, peak, and transition phases.
definition: Plan the Ski Jumping year: base, build, peak, and transition phases.
description: Season planning for Ski Jumping runs in phases: base (volume and technique), build (intensity and tactics), peak (sharpen for championships), transition (rest and play). One peak per season for most athletes; trying to peak year-round peaks never. Schedule deload weeks every 3-4 weeks — adaptation happens in recovery.

title: Tapering
d: Taper for Ski Jumping championships: cut volume 40-60%, keep intensity sharp.
definition: Taper for Ski Jumping championships: cut volume 40-60%, keep intensity sharp.
description: The Ski Jumping taper: 1-3 weeks out, cut training volume by 40 to 60 percent but keep some sharp intensity so the body stays awake. Sleep more, eat familiar food, trust the training. Most athletes taper too little and arrive flat, or train through and arrive tired — the taper is part of the program, not time off.

title: Youth development
d: Young Ski Jumping athletes: sample many sports, prioritize fun and fundamentals.
definition: Young Ski Jumping athletes: sample many sports, prioritize fun and fundamentals.
description: Youth Ski Jumping development: before age 14, multi-sport sampling beats early specialization for both skill and health. Keep sessions short, playful, and technique-rich; measure success in smiles and improvement, not trophies. Never year-round single-sport training before puberty — overuse injuries end more careers than opponents do.

title: Injury prevention
d: Prevent Ski Jumping injuries: warm up, strengthen the known weak links, manage load.
definition: Prevent Ski Jumping injuries: warm up, strengthen the known weak links, manage load.
description: Injury prevention in Ski Jumping targets the sport's known patterns: structured warm-ups (like FIFA 11+ style programs) cut injuries measurably, strength work protects joints, and load management — never spiking weekly volume more than about ten percent — prevents most overuse injuries. Report pain early; playing through sharp pain turns small problems into seasons lost.

title: Fitness testing
d: Test Ski Jumping fitness: repeat the same battery every 6-8 weeks.
definition: Test Ski Jumping fitness: repeat the same battery every 6-8 weeks.
description: Fitness testing for Ski Jumping: pick 4-6 tests covering speed, endurance, power, and sport skill, and repeat the identical battery every 6-8 weeks. Tests direct the program — train the weakest result. Record everything; athletes who test improve faster because the numbers make progress visible.

title: Return to play
d: Return to Ski Jumping after injury: criteria-based, not calendar-based.
definition: Return to Ski Jumping after injury: criteria-based, not calendar-based.
description: Return to Ski Jumping after injury follows criteria, not dates: full range of motion, strength symmetry, sport-specific movements pain-free, then controlled contact, then full training, then competition. Rushing back re-injures; the second injury is usually worse. Clearance from a clinician plus passing functional tests is the standard.

title: Pre-game routine
d: Ski Jumping pre-game: same timeline, same warm-up, same mindset every time.
definition: Ski Jumping pre-game: same timeline, same warm-up, same mindset every time.
description: The Ski Jumping pre-game routine: fixed timeline from arrival, dynamic warm-up progressing to sport speed, equipment check, tactical reminders, then quiet focus. Routines calm nerves by making the unfamiliar familiar. Rehearse the routine before minor events so it is automatic for major ones.

title: Video analysis
d: Study Ski Jumping film: your reps, opponents' tendencies, and elite models.
definition: Study Ski Jumping film: your reps, opponents' tendencies, and elite models.
description: Video analysis in Ski Jumping: review your own reps first (technique), then opponents (tendencies), then elite models (what great looks like). Keep clips short and specific — three clips with one fix each beats an hour of passive watching. Athletes who study film make better decisions under pressure.

title: Goal setting
d: Set Ski Jumping goals in three layers: outcome, performance, and process.
definition: Set Ski Jumping goals in three layers: outcome, performance, and process.
description: Goal setting for Ski Jumping: outcome goals (win the league) motivate, performance goals (improve first-touch success) direct, and process goals (today's drill focus) control the day. Write them down, review weekly, and keep process goals in the majority — athletes control effort and execution, not scoreboards.

title: Cross-training
d: Cross-train for Ski Jumping: swim, bike, or lift to build fitness without sport load.
definition: Cross-train for Ski Jumping: swim, bike, or lift to build fitness without sport load.
description: Cross-training for Ski Jumping keeps fitness growing while the sport-specific tissues rest: swimming for cardio without impact, cycling for legs without pounding, strength work for armor. One cross session weekly in season, more in the off-season. Variety also refreshes the mind — burnout ends more seasons than injuries do.

title: Equipment care
d: Ski Jumping gear lasts longer and performs better with basic maintenance.
definition: Ski Jumping gear lasts longer and performs better with basic maintenance.
description: Equipment care in Ski Jumping: clean it, dry it, store it right, and inspect it before every session. Worn gear causes injuries — dead shoes, frayed ropes, cracked helmets retire on schedule, not after failure. Keep a spare of anything that would end your day if it broke.

title: Travel competition
d: Travel for Ski Jumping events: control what you can — sleep, food, and warm-up.
definition: Travel for Ski Jumping events: control what you can — sleep, food, and warm-up.
description: Travel competition in Ski Jumping: arrive as early as the budget allows, bring familiar food, protect sleep across time zones, and scout the venue on arrival. Keep the pre-game routine identical to home — familiarity is calming. Pack backups of every critical item in carry-on.

title: Off-season
d: The Ski Jumping off-season: rest first, then rebuild the base and fix weaknesses.
definition: The Ski Jumping off-season: rest first, then rebuild the base and fix weaknesses.
description: The Ski Jumping off-season has two halves: complete rest for 2-4 weeks (mental and physical), then base rebuilding with high volume and low pressure. Fix the weakest link identified in testing, try a new sport for athleticism, and return to preseason hungry. Athletes who skip the off-season borrow from next year.
